case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease presented with multiple asymptomatic purpuric macules that had been persistent for more than 2 decades. The lesions began on the bilateral lower legs and extended to the inner thighs, with recent extension to the forearms. The lesions worsened with prolonged standing and were occasionally accompanied by mild itching. On examination, there were symmetrical diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules covering the legs (Figure 1) and forearms. The patient had no involvement of mucosal surfaces or nails, no positive family history of telangiectasias, and no clinical signs of systemic disease or bleeding diathesis. Dermoscopy revealed prominent fine telangiectasias, which was blanchable on pressure (Video).
case_info.caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
case_info.explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

The lesions began on the bilateral lower legs and extended to the inner thighs, with recent extension to the forearms. case_info.caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
case_info.explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.

Other options like Schamberg disease or hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia do not align well with the clinical picture provided.

[Doctor]: Given the benign nature of generalized essential telangiectasia, reassurance is usually the mainstay of management. I would inform the patient that while the lesions are not harmful and do not require treatment, they can be persistent. If the patient expresses cosmetic concerns or experiences discomfort, we could explore options like laser therapy or other modalities, but that's more of a secondary consideration. Overall, the focus should be on education and reassurance about the condition.
[AI Assistant]: Your management plan is sound and directly follows from the diagnosis. [NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

The lesions began on the bilateral lower legs and extended to the inner thighs, with recent extension to the forearms. case_info.caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
case_info.explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease presented with multiple asymptomatic purpuric macules that had been persistent for more than 2 decades. The lesions began on the bilateral lower legs and extended to the inner thighs, with recent extension to the forearms. The lesions worsened with prolonged standing and were occasionally accompanied by mild itching. On examination, there were symmetrical diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules covering the legs (Figure 1) and forearms. The patient had no involvement of mucosal surfaces or nails, no positive family history of telangiectasias, and no clinical signs of systemic disease or bleeding diathesis. case_info.caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
case_info.explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease presented with multiple asymptomatic purpuric macules that had been persistent for more than 2 decades. The lesions began on the bilateral lower legs and extended to the inner thighs, with recent extension to the forearms. The lesions worsened with prolonged standing and were occasionally accompanied by mild itching. On examination, there were symmetrical diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules covering the legs (Figure 1) and forearms. The patient had no involvement of mucosal surfaces or nails, no positive family history of telangiectasias, and no clinical signs of systemic disease or bleeding diathesis. Dermoscopy revealed prominent fine telangiectasias, which was blanchable on pressure (Video).
case_info.caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
case_info.explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,
    rounded to one decimal -- you may compute this, but the caller will also recompute it
    deterministically from your 4 integer scores>,
  "short_rationale": {

    "performance": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "effort": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "frustration": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>"
  }
}

case_info.caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
case_info.explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.

       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

       would be unsafe."

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
case_info.explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

The lesions began on the bilateral lower legs and extended to the inner thighs, with recent extension to the forearms. case_info.caption: Diffuse, blanchable, reticulated telangiectatic macules located on the left inner thigh.
case_info.explanation: Skin biopsy over the left lower leg revealed dilated small vessels in the upper dermis, along with amorphous concentric pink hyaline material deposited within the vessel walls, which had positive findings on periodic acid–Schiff staining but negative findings on Congo red staining (Figure 2). No signs of vasculitis or fibrin thrombi were seen. In the absence of systemic symptoms or involvement, observation was recommended, and the lesions remained stable at 3-month follow-up. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy (CCV) is a rare primary cutaneous microangiopathy that affects the superficial dermal blood vessels. It typically presents as asymptomatic telangiectasias or petechiae, primarily on the lower limbs, with a tendency to spread cephalically.1CCV occurs in middle-aged to older individuals with a nearly equal distribution between men and women, although it can also affect pediatric, middle-aged, and older patients.2Histologic features help distinguish CCV from similar clinical conditions. Typical CCV pathology shows dilated capillaries in the papillary and reticular dermis, along with perivascular deposits of hyaline material, which can be observed with periodic acid–Schiff staining. Pathogenesis suggests a pauci-inflammatory injury to endothelial cells caused by unknown angiogenic factors, leading to local intravascular fibrin thrombi.3Fibrin subsequently leaks and incorporates into the vessel walls, ultimately resulting in reparative perivascular fibrosis.3 Primary telangiectasias refer to idiopathic capillary dilation, which shares some clinical features with CCV. Both CCV and generalized essential telangiectasia present with the appearance of multiple symmetrical telangiectasias on the lower limbs, which gradually extend to the rest of the body. These conditions do not involve the mucosa or nail beds, and there are no preexisting lesions or associated systemic diseases, making clinical differentiation challenging.4However, histopathological examination of generalized essential telangiectasia typically demonstrate mild ectasia of thin-walled capillaries in the papillary dermis, without eosinophilic hyaline material within the vascular wall.5Schamberg disease predominantly affects men of any age, presenting as asymptomatic brownish macules and nonblanchable purpura or petechiae primarily located on the lower extremities with a characteristic cayenne pepper–speckling appearance.6Dermoscopy typically reveals red dots and red globules within a coppery brown background.7Histopathological findings of Schamberg disease include perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, reactive endothelial changes, extravasated red blood cells, and prominent hemosiderin-laden macrophages, which can be identified with an iron stain.8Venous insufficiency and chronic alcohol consumption appear to be related to the development of Schamberg disease.8Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations, commonly found on the hands, face, ears, lips, tongue, and inside the mouth. These lesions are often absent during childhood and typically increase with age, with the most common clinical manifestation being spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis.9Unlike CCV, individuals with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia exhibit mucosal and visceral involvement, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, along with a family history of similar telangiectatic processes or abnormal bleeding.9Histology reveals dilated small vascular channels in the affected organs.9Since extracutaneous involvement is extremely rare, the management of CCV currently focuses on local treatment due to cosmetic concerns, with pulsed dye laser therapy being the most effective approach.10 In conclusion, CCV has characteristic clinical and histopathological findings. Blanchable telangiectasias have perivascular hyaline deposits. The typical microscopic appearance can help distinguish CCV from clinical mimics.
